Tagma[^tagma-etym] is a computing primitive where the address *is* the coordinate — not a flat pointer, but a point in an N-dimensional geometric space. This is made possible by a 16-bit Unicode block allocated to a 3-axis writing system, which provides a collision-free, hash-less, structurally addressable coordinate space. Every valid 16-bit value in this space is simultaneously a 1-D address (Unicode code point), a 3-D coordinate (initial, medial, final), and a displayable Hangul syllable. This triple interpretation enables hash-less content addressing with zero collision probability and single-cycle combinational decoding at an estimated ~300 gates[^spec-status].

Every content-addressable system today generates identifiers through a hash function. SHA-256. UUID. Hash tables. This indirection layer imposes a predictable cost: gate area, cycle latency, storage overhead, and probabilistic collision resolution. The industry's answer has been faster hash units and larger hash tables -- never questioning whether hashing is needed at all. Tagma shows it is not. Where SHA-256 requires thousands of gates and dozens of cycles to generate a single identifier, Tagma does it in one cycle with an estimated ~300 gates. The identifier is not a random-looking hex string -- it is a pronounceable syllable that carries its own coordinate system.

```{python}
#| include: false
import numpy as np

n_init, n_med, n_fin = 19, 21, 28
stride = 2
init_vals = np.arange(0, n_init, stride)
med_vals  = np.arange(0, n_med,  stride)
fin_vals  = np.arange(0, n_fin,  stride)

I, M, F = np.meshgrid(init_vals, med_vals, fin_vals, indexing='ij')
I_f, M_f, F_f = [a.flatten() for a in (I, M, F)]

def box_edges(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1):
    edges = []
    def add(xa, ya, za, xb, yb, zb):
        edges.append(((xa, ya, za), (xb, yb, zb)))
    for (dx, dy, dz) in [(x1,y0,z0),(x0,y1,z0),(x0,y0,z1)]:
        add(x0,y0,z0,dx,dy,dz)
    add(x1,y1,z0, x1,y0,z0); add(x1,y1,z0, x0,y1,z0); add(x1,y1,z0, x1,y1,z1)
    add(x0,y1,z1, x1,y1,z1); add(x0,y1,z1, x0,y0,z1); add(x0,y1,z1, x0,y1,z0)
    add(x1,y0,z1, x1,y1,z1); add(x1,y0,z1, x1,y0,z0); add(x1,y0,z1, x0,y0,z1)
    return edges

full_edges  = box_edges(0, 0, 0, 31, 31, 31)
valid_edges = box_edges(0, 0, 0, 18, 20, 27)
```

## The primitive hidden in a writing system

Unicode assigns each script a fixed address block. Within this block, Hangul occupies a contiguous 16-bit segment (U+AC00--U+D7AF) invented in 1443 and allocated in Unicode 2.0 in 1996. Its composition formula embeds three independent structural axes into every code point:

$$C(i,m,f) = \text{U+AC00} + 588i + 28m + f$$
$$\quad (0 \leq i < 19,\; 0 \leq m < 21,\; 0 \leq f < 28)$$

Every valid 16-bit value carries three simultaneous interpretations: a 1-D Unicode address, a 3-D coordinate, and a Hangul syllable. A hardware decoder extracts these fields in a single combinational cycle at an estimated ~300 gate equivalents -- smaller than a single 32-bit multiplier. Of the 65,536 possible 16-bit values in this range, 11,172 are structurally valid (matching the composition formula), and the remaining 54,364 are immediately detectable as invalid by the same logic.

These three axes are the atomic building block of an abstract N-dimensional coordinate algebra whose semantics are entirely application-defined. CoordPath chains multiple syllables to reach arbitrarily high dimensions (6 syllables = 18 axes, 19 syllables = 57 axes), and every axis position can represent a different categorical dimension -- region, device type, timestamp, shard, or any other application-level concept. The arithmetic operations (composition, decomposition, Hamming distance, axis projection) are invariant; only the axis interpretation changes per deployment.

No other Unicode script satisfies all four conditions required: a contiguous fixed-width 16-bit address range, a closed-form composition formula, a complete three-axis decomposition, and an open international standard. Hangul is unique.

## The cost of hashing: what Tagma removes

Every hash-based identity system consumes energy and area before producing a single useful result. A SHA-256 engine requires approximately 10,000 gates and 64-75 cycles per operation, then needs a hash table, collision resolution, and dynamic resizing. UUID generation requires entropy collection and still delivers probabilistic uniqueness with 128-bit identifiers expressed as 36 hex characters.

Tagma replaces all of this with a combinational decoder and a 16-bit register. The output is not an opaque hex string but a readable Hangul syllable -- or a sequence of syllables for larger spaces. A single syllable covers 11,172 identifiers. Six syllables (18 axes) cover $1.9 \times 10^{24}$ identifiers, exceeding typical distributed system needs. Nineteen syllables match the full SHA-256 space of $2^{256}$. At every scale, the identifier is human-readable, self-validating, and free of special characters.

The measured software cost on an Apple M1: 2 ns for a single-syllable identifier versus 227 ns for SHA-256 (115x faster). At SHA-256 scale (19 syllables): 35 ns versus 227 ns (6.5x faster). These figures only compare identifier generation (write). On every subsequent access (read), the gap becomes immeasurable: Tagma retrieves data through direct array indexing, a single deterministic operation, while hash-based systems require hash computation, collision resolution, and multiple memory dereferences -- fundamentally nondeterministic access paths. In dedicated silicon, the generation gap is expected to widen further because the per-syllable decoder would require only a single combinational cycle independent of syllable count.

## Verification by exhaustive enumeration

The Tagma coordinate space is exhaustively enumerable: 65,536 possible 16-bit values, of which exactly 11,172 satisfy the composition formula. A verification harness generates all 65,536 inputs, applies the decoder specification, and records every result. The bijection is verified by enumeration: no collisions, no unassigned values within the block. Every implementation, hardware or software, can be verified against the same ground truth in milliseconds on any commodity system.

This is not possible with hash-based systems. A SHA-256 engine cannot be exhaustively verified across its full input space. Tagma can, because its coordinate space is bounded and its formula is closed-form.

## Application domains

**Embedded and sensor systems.** The 11,172-identifier space fits entirely in a single no-allocator array of 22 KB (89 KB for 64-bit values). Every Coord is a direct array index: one load, no hashing, no collisions, no resizing. A zero-initialized array gives bulk operations a 15x advantage over HashMap for this class of use.

**LLM inference cache.** Key-value caches indexed by token sequence prefixes currently use hash tables or radix trees. Tagma replaces this with CoordPath-based direct access: each prefix maps to a unique CoordPath, lookup cost is O(1) direct array accesses with zero hash computation. Production cache sizes (typically $10^4$--$10^7$ entries) are covered by 2--4 syllables.

**Graph and multi-dimensional query.** Each node maps to a Coord, each edge type to a CoordSet. Adjacency reduces to a single bitwise AND over 175 machine words. Multi-dimensional queries project directly to axis ranges without index intersection, with cost independent of graph size.

**General-purpose content addressing.** Wherever UUIDs, hash keys, or sequence-number identifiers are used today -- database records, distributed nodes, file identifiers, commit hashes -- Tagma provides a shorter, faster, human-readable alternative with zero collision probability.

## Boundaries

Tagma does not replace cryptographic primitives. SHA-256 remains for signatures, Merkle proofs, and preimage resistance. Encryption, authentication, and key derivation are outside its scope. Tagma replaces the use of hashes as structural identifiers and addresses. The two can also be combined: SHA-256 output encoded as 19 Hangul syllables is more readable than 64 hex characters while preserving the same $2^{-256}$ collision probability.

Tagma is built on open international standards and will run on open ISA (RISC-V) -- unencumbered by proprietary licensing or regional dependencies. It is a neutral, sovereign primitive for the global computing landscape.

## 588년 전의 설계, 데이터 주소 체계가 되다

1443년 창제된 한글은 초성 19, 중성 21, 종성 28이라는 세 독립 축의 조합으로 음절을 구성합니다. 이 완성형 음절은 예외 규칙이 없으며, 유니코드 표준(U+AC00–U+D7AF)에서 16비트 고정 공간에 연속적으로 배정되어 있습니다. 동시에 초성·중성·종성의 조합 원리는 그대로 3차원 좌표 표현이 됩니다. 더욱이 이 공간은 유니코드 기본 정의 공간(BMP, Plane 0)에 속해 있어, 모든 컴퓨팅 인프라 계층에서 별도 설정 없이도 오류 없이 다뤄지며 인간이 식별 가능한 음절로 해석됩니다. 이는 아파트 동-호수 체계와 쉽게 비유할 수 있으며, 건물의 층수와 호실 배열이 일관되게 정의되어 있다면, "101호"라는 주소만으로 중앙 안내판(해시 테이블) 없이 즉시 해당 방의 위치를 알 수 있습니다. Tagma는 한글 음절 좌표를 이와 같은 원리로, 모든 컴퓨팅 인프라와 컴파일러가 공통으로 사용하는 국제 유니코드 표준을 주소 표준으로 활용하는 체계입니다.

Tagma는 이 네 가지 조건—(1) 16비트 고정 공간, (2) 완전한 조합 구조, (3) 코드 포인트에 반영된 3축 좌표, (4) 국제 표준(ISO/IEC 10646) 공공재—이 모두 겹치는 덕분에 성립하는 수학적 기반위에 해시 함수 없이도 충돌 없는 무한한 식별자 공간을 생성하는 점을 이용해, 근본적인 데이터 처리 방식을 실제 다양한 소프트웨어와 하드웨어 계층의 구현을 통해 이를 모든 컴퓨팅 분야에 적용하는 프로젝트 입니다. 따라서 산술 연산만으로 데이터 주소를 추출하고 직접 접근하기 때문에 비교 불가능한 성능 향상을 달성하며, 좌표계의 기하학적 특성 덕분에 기존의 기하학적 공학 이론을 즉시 적용할 수 있습니다. 이는 기존의 암호화 체계를 대체하는 것이 아니라, 보완할 수 있는 계층으로 매우 단순한 원리 덕분에 기존의 암호화 알고리즘과 친화적인 연동성과 확장성이 보장됩니다.
